title: What changed in Soap Creek Valley?
description: Follow a vanished town, a resident’s memory of Camp Adair, and the work of managing a research forest. These are different witnesses to a changing landscape.

image.alt: Historic photograph of the Moore family farm beside Soap Creek.
image.caption: The Moore family farm on Soap Creek, about 1899 or 1900. Photograph by Samuel H. Moore.
image.credit: Courtesy of Myra Moore Lauridson and the Soap Creek Schoolhouse Foundation, as credited on Bob Zybach’s original site.

steps.title: Where did the town go?
steps.instruction: Read Bob’s short 1989 account of Tampico. Notice the difference between a place that disappears and stories that survive.
steps.label: Tampico: Auto Tour stop 5

steps.title: What did change feel like to a resident?
steps.instruction: Read Velma Carter Rawie’s answer on page 43. Her response to Camp Adair is a personal judgment; keep her voice distinct from the tour writer’s account.
steps.label: Velma Carter Rawie, page 43

steps.title: Who else remembered Camp Adair?
steps.instruction: Open the Camp Adair place page and follow one other narrator’s page reference. Compare what each person chose to remember.
steps.label: Camp Adair: map and recollections

steps.title: What can a fallen tree tell you?
steps.instruction: Hear Bob Zybach and Marvin Rowley discuss hardwoods, roots and soil. Follow the printed words, examine the original page and see Rowley in the forest. What would you want to check on the ground?
steps.label: Listen and read with Bob and Marvin Rowley
steps.secondaryLabel: Read Rowley on the earlier forest management work

related.label: Follow the same valley into Letitia Carson’s records
related.instruction: A century earlier, the Carson story survives in papers about this same valley.

title: What does Letitia Carson’s court record show?
description: Follow a claim, an answer and two jury decisions. The spelling is the clerks’ own; Jan and John Meranda made the transcriptions.

image.alt: Open farmland and wooded hills in Soap Creek Valley.
image.caption: Soap Creek Valley in 1993, photographed by Bob Zybach.
image.credit: From Bob Zybach’s published Letitia Carson research at orww.org.

steps.title: What did she ask the court to recognize?
steps.instruction: Read the September 1854 complaint on page 14. What work does it describe, over what years, and what payment does it seek?
steps.label: The complaint, page 14

steps.title: How did the administrator answer?
steps.instruction: Read Green B. Smith’s answer on page 21. Separate what he alleged from what the court later decided. This page contains his assertion that Letitia was enslaved.
steps.label: The answer, page 21

steps.title: What did the first jury decide?
steps.instruction: Read the May 1855 judgment on pages 32–33. Then use the document register to find the original scan: transcription and image are two ways of checking the record.
steps.label: The first judgment, pages 32–33

steps.title: What happened in the later case?
steps.instruction: Read the October 1856 jury decision on page 61. Compare the second decision with the first; follow the adjacent papers if you want the fuller case.
steps.label: The later jury decision, page 61

related.label: How to cite a page in the Library
related.instruction: Keep a permanent link to the exact page you used.

title: What can one forest stop reveal?
description: Visit Dean Mountain on film, then return to an earlier interview and the photographs taken on that earlier tour. The place connects the records; the recordings were made on different dates.

image.alt: A concrete remnant and grass at a foggy Dean Mountain stop.
image.caption: Deans Mountain, frame 0989, November 8, 2017. Place and date from the creator’s catalog.
image.credit: From Bob Zybach’s ORWW Elliott files; no separate photographer credit is recorded for this frame.

steps.title: What do you see from the lookout?
steps.instruction: Watch the Dean’s Mountain Lookout stop, beginning at 10:46. Stop at 13:54 if you are following the short trail.
steps.label: The 2020 field trip: 10:46–13:54

steps.title: What did the earlier visitors remember?
steps.instruction: Read pages 140–141 of the November 2017 interview. David Gould and Jerry Phillips discuss the Civilian Conservation Corps road and earlier forest work; Bob asks whether they would make the same management choices again.
steps.label: The 2017 interview, pages 140–141
steps.secondaryLabel: Hear the original voices and follow the text (5:08)

steps.title: Can the photograph sharpen your reading?
steps.instruction: Look at the Dean Mountain photographs, including frame 0990 from the 2017 tour. Compare the view with the interview and the later film; do not assume every image records the same moment.
steps.label: Dean Mountain: map, records and photographs

steps.title: Why is the Elliott in a school-trust library?
steps.instruction: Read the collection’s explanation of the Elliott’s connection to the Common School Fund, then use the Library’s Oregon page for the wider school-trust record.
steps.label: The Elliott’s school-trust connection

title: How do we compare accounts of 1828?
description: Read an expedition journal, a company report and a chief’s account preserved by a company officer. Ask who spoke, who wrote, and what each source can tell us.

image.alt: Henry Warre’s painting of Fort Vancouver.
image.caption: Fort Vancouver, painted by Henry Warre in 1845 or 1846, as dated in Bob Zybach’s caption.
image.credit: Creator’s scan; caption source: Bob Zybach, illustration captions, May 29, 2023.

steps.title: What survives from the people involved?
steps.instruction: Scan the primary-source list. Notice which items are journals, which are reports, and which scans have no searchable text. A document’s date and author help define what it can support.
steps.label: The primary-source shelf

steps.title: What did Rogers and McLoughlin record?
steps.instruction: Read the passages Bob selected for the interpretive sign, especially Rogers on July 12 and McLoughlin’s August report. Notice the distinction between a journal entry and a report made after the event.
steps.label: Journal and report passages

steps.title: How does the chief’s account reach us?
steps.instruction: Read the account given by Chief St. Arnoose and recorded by Alexander McLeod on October 11. Compare the explanation with the previous passages, remembering that a company officer wrote these words down.
steps.label: The account recorded from Chief St. Arnoose

steps.title: What remains unsettled?
steps.instruction: Use the chronology to see where dates and numbers disagree. Follow one citation back to its source before deciding which version you would repeat.
steps.label: Dates, sources and disagreements

related.label: Keep the source with your quotation
related.instruction: Use the work’s citation and the page link, and distinguish the original speaker from the person who recorded the account.
